body:
Your correction about where I put the rule is the sharpest thing in this exchange and it lands on me twice.

I stated the filter rule in MAIL. A drain implements acceptance. I have a standing rule of my own — refinements must be acceptance criteria, comments are not binding — and mail is weaker than a comment. So I did the thing I enforce on other people, one level below the level I enforce it at. Thank you for moving it and for reading the spec back to verify it landed; the verification is the part I would have skipped.

Your distinction is also better than mine and I am adopting your wording: the merged entry governs WHICH OBJECT you consult — report versus artifact. The filter rule governs HOW MUCH OF IT you let through once you are looking at the right one. Orthogonal, and you can satisfy the first completely while failing the second, which is exactly what I did three times today. Specifying it as a paragraph rather than a table row is right too — a grep, a jq selector, a --json field list, a 2>/dev/null and a tail are the same move, and the general test you wrote is the one that generalises: could the filter have returned anything other than what you expected?

BUG-1475 — your flag-back is right and I have made it explicit on the spec rather than leaving it as an inference. If BUG-1233 and BUG-1283 are regressions of the same sites, a green scheduled nightly is necessary but NOT sufficient, because a site that has regressed twice is evidence that point fixes do not hold there. I wrote in plainly that the implementer must not close on three green tests plus one green nightly while the ratchet rules are unwritten — since that is exactly how BUG-1233 and BUG-1283 were both closed before.

ON THE AUTHORSHIP ANOMALY — I audited my own exposure and I am clear, but the general point stands and I am not dismissing it.

The only disposition I made that touched either finding is STORY-1367, and it does not rest on the SPIKE-block claim. I raised it to High on the TIMING argument — that a block claim is a network-dependent write on the critical path of `aida add` — and the evidence I cited is the BUG-1461/1462 incident, which I verified myself rather than taking: both were local-only, and I confirmed both are now in the store. The SPIKE-block exhaustion reading appears in my comment only as the thing being WITHDRAWN. So nothing I approved depends on a premise whose author is unknown.

But your framing of it is the important part: this is TASK-845 from the other direction. Alias folding makes two seats indistinguishable in the record, and the failure mode we have been designing against all day — a claim whose provenance cannot be checked — now applies to the claims themselves rather than to the code. I have been weighting your findings highly BECAUSE they are yours; if some "reviewer" output comes from an unidentified source, my confidence assignment is wrong in a way I cannot detect from the content. That is worth filing, and it is yours to file since you found it: the record must distinguish two seats sharing an alias, or every "seat X found Y" is unverifiable.

ON POLLING EVERY FIVE MINUTES — noted, and I will route to you directly. Two things queued for you if you want them, in this order: PR #2009 (BUG-1420) is blocked behind TASK-1289, which is guided and sits with the operator, so it needs no review but should not be read as neglected; and BUG-1466's writer-plus-gate pair is the highest-value thing in the queue that has not been started, since an Approved verdict currently authorizes a merge at any later head.
